Our finding that changes in workplace design affect electronic and F2F interaction networks differently (and, on some measures, in opposite directions) should make future researchers wary of using one network as a proxy for the other.

limitations: The study is limited to two corporate headquarters, potentially limiting generalizability to other organizations or office designs.
The proposed mechanism of social withdrawal is inferred from interaction patterns rather than directly measured (e.g., through surveys on privacy perception or psychological states).
The study primarily focuses on the volume of interaction, not the quality or content of collaboration.
The latent space model finding that physical distance affected F2F interaction twice as much as email interaction is mentioned but not fully detailed in the main results tables.
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated the impact of transitioning to open office architectures on human collaboration patterns in two corporate headquarters. Contrary to common belief, the findings revealed a significant decrease (approximately 70%) in face-to-face interaction, accompanied by a substantial increase in electronic communication (email and instant messaging). The authors suggest this shift reflects a natural human response to socially withdraw from officemates in open environments, likely due to privacy concerns or cognitive overload. Limitations include the generalizability of findings from two case studies, the inferential nature of the social withdrawal mechanism, and the focus on interaction volume rather than quality.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Organizations’ pursuit of increased workplace collaboration has led managers to transform traditional office spaces into ‘open’, transparency-enhancing architectures with fewer walls, doors and other spatial boundaries, yet there is scant direct empirical research on how human interaction patterns change as a result of these architectural changes. In two intervention-based field studies of corporate headquarters transitioning to more open office spaces, we empirically examined—using digital data from advanced wearable devices and from electronic communication servers—the effect of open office architectures on employees' face-to-face, email and instant messaging (IM) interaction patterns. Contrary to common belief, the volume of face-to-face interaction decreased significantly (approx. 70%) in both cases, with an associated increase in electronic interaction. In short, rather than prompting increasingly vibrant face-to-face collaboration, open architecture appeared to trigger a natural human response to socially withdraw from officemates and interact instead over email and IM. This is the first study to empirically measure both face-to-face and electronic interaction before and after the adoption of open office architecture. The results inform our understanding of the impact on human behaviour of workspaces that trend towards fewer spatial boundaries.This article is part of the theme issue ‘Interdisciplinary approaches for uncovering the impacts of architecture on collective behaviour’.
